title: per-socket-pstate-and-kernel-selection-playbook
content:
Purpose and scope:

This is a working playbook for per-socket P-state (clock/power) policies and runtime kernel-selection heuristics for our inference serving runtime. It codifies lessons from microbenchmarks across A100, H100, L4, and MI300 and ties those to practical scheduling, KV cache partitioning, and telemetry that the platform can use to make deterministic, low-cost routing decisions. This doc is intentionally pragmatic — operational knobs, safe defaults, and an experiment matrix for when to deviate.

Audience:
- Serving runtime engineers implementing scheduler/kernel selection
- Platform engineers operating mixed GPU pools
- SREs who triage performance regressions in production

Quick TL;DR recommendations (safe defaults):
- Default P-state policy: conservative boost: set sustained_power_limit to 85% of vendor TDP for mixed-tenant pools, 95–100% on dedicated pools for strict-latency workloads.
- Clocking for NVIDIA: use nvidia-smi persistent application clocks via nvidia-smi -ac for stable kernel latencies; avoid dynamic auto-boost when latency SLOs < 50ms.
- Clocking for AMD MI300: pin compute clocks via roc-smi / radeon-smi equivalent (vendor tools) where available and monitor SM activity to avoid thermal throttles.
- Kernel selection: choose attention/FFN kernel variant by (dtype, seq_len_bucket, batch_size). Maintain a lightweight kernel-profile cache keyed on (model_id, dtype, seq_len_bucket, hw_capabilities).
- KV cache partitioning: prefer per-GPU MVAPICH-style partitioning when requests have long prefix reuse; prefer shared KV (host pinned memory or NVMe cache) for very large context models when memory pressure is high.

1) Terms and buckets used in the playbook
- seq_len_bucket: tiny(<=64), short(65-256), medium(257-1024), long(>1024)
- dtype buckets: fp16, bf16, int8 (quantized)
- hw_capabilities: {tensor_cores, sparse_support, mfma_capable (MI300)}
- workload shapes: steady_stream, microburst, cold_start

2) Why per-socket P-states matter for serving
- Dynamic DVFS and auto-boost produce variance in kernel latency due to frequency jitter and thermal throttling. For short critical requests (latency SLOs < 100ms) this variance dominates.
- Setting a predictable sustained clock removes frequency tail events and lets scheduler correlate kernel choices with measured performance.

3) Practical clock/power knobs by hardware family
- NVIDIA (A100/H100/L4):
  - Use nvidia-smi -pm 1 to enable persistence, then nvidia-smi -ac <memClock,graphicsClock> to stick to application clocks where available.
  - For A100 with MIG: consider instance sizing before clocking as MIG slices have different optimal clock regimes.
  - For L4 (edge-focused): prioritize lower graphics clocks but maintain high SM clocks when integer/FP mixed workloads dominate.
  - Avoid global throttling: prefer setting sustained_power_limit via nvidia-smi -pl rather than letting the driver aggress on clocks.
- AMD (MI300):
  - Use vendor SMI to set sustained performance states where possible. There are differences across ROCm releases; always validate with microbenchmarks.
  - Watch for HBM thermal hotspots — voltage scaling can produce sudden latency spikes under bursty loads.

4) Kernel selection policy (high level)
- Inputs: model_id, dtype, seq_len, batch_size, hw_capabilities, current_clock_state, observed_util/latency_histogram
- Process: map seq_len -> seq_len_bucket; query kernel_profile_cache for best kernel; if no entry, fallback order: flash-attn-optimized kernel -> tensor-core fused kernel -> reference kernel.
- Update kernel_profile_cache asynchronously using background microbenchmarks on the live instance (safe read-only probing, low-priority CUDA streams).
- Cost signal: prefer int8/bf16 kernels when they pass quality checks for the model. Use our Optimize recommendations to pick quantization profiles per-model.

5) Scheduler integration and preemption
- Use CUDA stream priorities + per-GPU priority queues to isolate latency-critical requests. Priority mapping: realtime (user-facing <50ms SLO) -> high, batch/async -> low.
- For mixed workload servers, set a per-GPU reservation (a soft quota) of SM/TX capacity for high-priority streams to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- Consider driver-level isolation (MPS with priority streams) for H100/A100 where supported. When MIG is available, create small MIG instances for high-priority lanes.

6) KV cache placement and partitioning heuristics
- If per-request prefix reuse > 60% and KV memory per-request < 10% of GPU RAM -> colocate KV on-GPU per-process to maximize reuse and avoid PCIe/PCIEe transfers.
- If context windows are massive (>70% of GPU RAM) or model uses extremely large KV (multi-million tokens), use sharded KV across multiple GPUs with an index on the host for routing.
- For dedicated pools with predictable traffic, pre-populate KV on devices during warmup windows. For bursty traffic, fall back to host-pinned KV with an LRU that favors active prefixes.

7) Telemetry signals to drive dynamic policies (list of recommended metrics)
- per-GPU: SM utilization (with per-SM breakdown), PCIe/HHB transfer rates, power draw (W), temperature (C), clock (MHz), persistence state, throttle_count
- per-kernel: median p50/p95 latency, kernel occupancy, achieved TFLOPS (or ops/s), memory bandwidth utilization
- workload signals: request size distribution, prefix_reuse_rate, batch_coalescing_rate
- Thresholds to trigger a policy change: sustained p95 latency increase > 15% for 5 minutes, power draw within 5W of sustained_power_limit for > 30s, or sudden drops in tensor-core utilization > 20%

8) Microbenchmark matrix (summary of most useful experiments)
- Matrix axes: hardware x dtype x seq_len_bucket x batch_size x clock_setting
- Run: 10k short inferences (tiny/short buckets) with cold/warm KV, measure p50/p95, variance, and thermal trend
- Example finding (sanity check): On A100, flash-attn kernel at 95% TDP reduced p95 by ~18% for medium sequence lengths vs default auto-boost; on L4, lowering graphics clocks by 10% reduced power by 12% while p95 for int8 workloads increased only 3% (acceptable for batch scoring).

9) Operational runbook snippets
- Diagnose high tail latency: check per-GPU throttle_count, clock jitter, and kernel_profile_cache hit rate. If throttle_count > 0: drop sustained_power_limit by 5% and re-evaluate — thermal throttles may be masking as scheduler faults.
- Re-provisioning guidance: for latency-sensitive queues seeing microburst drops, spin up dedicated smaller-instance MIG slices (when possible) or move them to dedicated reserved capacity.

10) Kernel-profile cache spec (simple key/value)
- Key: model_id|dtype|seq_len_bucket|hw_family|clock_profile_name
- Value: kernel_id, observed_p50, observed_p95, last_tested_utc, notes
- Eviction: LRU by last_tested_utc; keep entries for active models pinned.

11) Safety, regression and validation checks
- Always validate quantized kernels against golden output set for a small prompt suite before routing production traffic.
- When updating sustained_power_limit on a node, run a short warmup and collect p95 for 2k requests before rolling to full pool.

12) Open questions and next experiments (TODOs)
- Better automated per-GPU ML model to predict kernel choice from telemetry (investigate decision tree vs small NN).
- Policy to auto-fallback from on-GPU KV to host-shared KV that minimizes extra latency for mid-size contexts.
- Formalize MIG sizing guidance for H100 (driver-dependent) across ROCm/NVIDIA driver versions.

Appendix: commands and quick checks (examples)- NVIDIA: nvidia-smi -pm 1; nvidia-smi -pl <watts>; nvidia-smi -ac <memClock,graphicsClock>
- AMD: (example, vendor tools vary) radeon-smi --showclocks; rocm-smi --setperflevel high (validate on release)
- Kernel probe pattern (background low-priority): launch a short micro-run on cudaStreamNonBlocking with priority low and record counters

Notes on provenance: experiments referenced above were run on internal perf-lab nodes between 2024-09 and 2025-01. Raw CSVs and scripts are linked in linked_artifacts.

Contact: Aisha Patel (eng-serving-runtime) for questions and to request experiments.

End of draft.
